message: I run a community screening programme and I'm drafting the letter that goes to people with a positive result. Among the people we screen, about 1% actually have the condition. The test picks up 90% of true cases, and 9% of people who don't have the condition test positive anyway. Our analyst, Dev, says that of everyone who tests positive, fewer than 1 in 10 actually have the condition, so the letter shouldn't say "you probably have it" but should say a follow-up test is needed. My deputy thinks that can't be right: "the test is about 90% accurate, so a positive should mean roughly a 90% chance". I tend to agree with Dev, but it feels strange to send a letter that says a positive result usually means nothing is wrong. Can we go with Dev's wording?
response:
**Yes, Dev is right.** The numbers work out to about a 9% chance that someone with a positive result actually has the condition.

## The arithmetic

Picture 10,000 people screened:

| | Have the condition | Don't have it | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| People | 100 (1%) | 9,900 | 10,000 |
| Test positive | 90 (90% of 100) | 891 (9% of 9,900) | **981** |
| Test negative | 10 | 9,009 | 9,019 |

Of the 981 positives, only 90 have the condition: **90 ÷ 981 ≈ 9.2%**. That's a bit under 1 in 10, as Dev said.

## Where your deputy's intuition goes wrong

"90% accurate" describes how the test performs *within each group*: it catches 90% of true cases and correctly clears 91% of healthy people. It doesn't tell you what a positive result means for an individual. That depends heavily on how common the condition is. Because 99% of the people screened are healthy, even a small 9% false-positive rate applied to that large group (891 people) swamps the true positives from the small sick group (90 people). This is often called the base-rate fallacy, and it's very common, including among clinicians.

## On the letter's wording

I'd go with Dev's substance but frame it carefully. "A positive result usually means nothing is wrong" is technically close to true, but it may lead people to skip the follow-up, which would defeat the purpose of screening. A positive result raises someone's chance from about 1% to about 9%, roughly nine times higher, so the follow-up genuinely matters.

Something like:

> *Your screening result was positive. This does **not** mean you have [condition]. Screening tests are designed to catch as many cases as possible, so many people who receive a positive result turn out not to have it. In fact, most people with a positive screening result are found to be clear after further testing. However, a positive result does mean we need to look more closely, so it is important that you attend a follow-up test. [How to book / what happens next.]*

This is accurate, reduces unnecessary alarm, and still gives a clear reason to act.

One more point that may be useful: a **negative** result is very reassuring here. Only about 10 in 9,019 negatives (around 0.1%) are missed cases, so you can say that confidently in the negative-result letter.
